connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: Connecting singular to a ledger provider.

Dated qualification, 2026-10-15: rejection after the window, rejection before the deadline, request value and refund routing, rejection and retraction refund controls, and rejection inside the processing and retraction windows are all unmet by ruling: implementation follows the superseded rule; the ruled rule is not implemented. The live comparisons still exercise the legacy rejection that spends the registry state output. The ruled rejection reads that output by reference and never spends it. Agreement with the legacy path is not acceptance of the ruled design. The earlier processing-window consumer requirement and the unresolved refund-routing requirement remain open. Historical results below retain their original revision and evidence binding; they do not establish current acceptance.

As a registry operator, you create a registry through singular state create and sign and submit bundles through singular wallet and singular submit. You also use create, insert, update, terminate, fold and inspect through open-datum, with a Koios API on your chosen network. The commands that create a registry and book, fold, reclaim and clean up a registration are described in create a registry and register keys on the proved design. You supply the API settings and pinned time material; each write is signed from your vault, or by a signer elsewhere through a bundle file (see Signing a write elsewhere, or from your vault). Commands read raw facts through one logical session, build and evaluate locally, submit signed transactions, and preserve recovery evidence in the registry journal.
Words such as registry, state token, request, fold, window, vault and bundle are explained as they first appear in the step-by-step page of singular-demo; the Demo 1 page tells the story in short.

The ordinary provider is Koios. Old backend and socket settings are refused before acquisition or registry effects. The current provider session promises no coherent chain snapshot and carries no verification witness.

asking-the-program-for-help.text: As a registry operator, you can ask either program what it does before you read this page or any other. singular --version and open-datum --version print the program's name, its version and the commit it was built from; a build that carries no commit says commit unknown. singular --help and open-datum --help print one screen: what the program is for, and every command with a line about it. Each command has its own --help that shows only that command: its settings, each with a description and a default, the signer routes grouped with the vault first and the key file, which is legacy, last, the environment variables it reads, an example for a command that writes, and how it ends.

A mistyped command or flag prints what is wrong in one line, the usage of the command you were heading for and where its help is, and exits with status 2. A mistyped command also names the nearest command. A failure that no command reported itself, such as a file that cannot be read, ends as one line on standard error saying what failed, with status 1, never the runtime's own report of an uncaught exception. Both programs complete commands and flags in your shell: source <(singular --bash-completion-script "$(which singular)") for bash, with --zsh-completion-script and --fish-completion-script for the other shells.

The overview of each program follows, quoted from the program itself. The first line of every help page names the version and the commit; it is left out here, and VERSION stands for the version of the build. The documentation check runs the programs and fails when a quotation, or the settings table below, disagrees with what they print.

the-settings-you-give.text: The URL, network magic and one signer (the signing key, the vault, or on singular create, singular fold, singular reclaim, singular reject, open-datum create, open-datum insert, open-datum update, open-datum terminate and open-datum fold an address with its bundle file) travel together on a write: naming only some of them is refused as partially configured, and so is a write that names none, because singular never starts a node of its own — a registry booted on a chain that dies with the process could not be attached to again. The refusal says which part is missing and, for the signer, the three ways to name one: the vault first, then an address with its bundle file, and last the key file, which is legacy. The settings that do not change from one command to the next (the node, the contracts, the registry, the token file, the narration and the vault) can be given once, as the next section says; the key file, an external signer and everything else a command does are typed on the command. Public environment configuration lists the variables and the phase-log path.

The file alice.json is the key's payload, ordinary JSON stored as plain JSON unless --payload-schema detailed says it is written in the detailed Plutus data schema; store ordinary JSON as a key's payload gives the rules.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: Giving the chain, the contracts and the registry once.

As a registry operator, you type the same six settings on nearly every command: the Koios address, the network magic and the pinned time directory (the chain), the blueprint (the compiled contracts), and the state directory and the state token, or the registry's address, which holds the state token and the network (the registry). You can write them once. Each has three forms, and the first one that is present wins.

The variable is SINGULAR_ followed by the flag's name in capitals with underscores, and the key is the flag's name without its dashes. The six above are --koios-url, --network-time, --network-magic, --blueprint, --state-dir and --state-token. Six more have the same three forms: --registry, --koios-token-file, the narration controls --trace, --trace-to and --trace-format, and --vault. The --help of every command lists the three forms of each of them that the command takes, and says where the config file is.

The config file is one JSON object. Both programs read the same file: it is singular.json in the folder you run the command from, or the file named by --config FILE or by the variable SINGULAR_CONFIG. With a file like this in your demo folder, open-datum insert --key alice --payload payload.json --vault alice.vault is a whole command, and it does exactly what the same command with the six flags does:
What you see when something is wrong:
A missing setting is refused in the usual line, missing --koios-url, and below it one line names the flag, the variable and the key that would give it.

A file that does not exist when you named it, that is not JSON, that is not one object, or that holds a key the program does not read is refused in one sentence naming the file. A key that is nearly a setting's name says which one it nearly is. A default singular.json that is not there is no file; one that is there and broken is refused. A problem with the file never stops --help or --version.
A path in the file means what the same path means on the command line: it is read from the folder the command runs from.
A value is text or a number, as network-magic above; an empty text or null is no setting.

Nothing else can come from the file or the environment. The key file, an external signer, the passphrase and what a command does stay on the command line: a file that names a passphrase is refused, and the passphrase stays on the terminal prompt or on the descriptor --passphrase-fd names. The environment gives a passphrase only on a development network, as SINGULAR_PASSPHRASE; the section after the vault one says how.
A line that carries every flag it needs means what it meant before. An environment variable or a file only fills in what the line leaves out, so a flag you type is never overruled.

the-registrys-name-kept-by-create.text: The registry's name kept by create.

As Alice, I create a registry and act on it next, and I do not want to copy its state token out of the receipt. I add the switch --save-state-token to create, and the command keeps the name for me. The example below creates a registry on the development network and asks for its name to be kept.

When the create succeeds, the command writes the new registry's state token into the settings file as the key state-token, and says on standard error which file now holds it. open-datum create takes the same switch. The next commands find the state token there, and the other settings in the same file when it already holds them, as in the section above. With a file that holds the chain and the contracts, open-datum fold --vault alice.vault and open-datum insert --key alice --payload payload.json --vault alice.vault name no registry on their line.

The file is the one the other commands read: the file named by --config, else the one named by SINGULAR_CONFIG, else singular.json in the folder the command runs from. When none of the three exists as a file, create makes singular.json there, holding the one key. Every other key keeps its value and its kind, text or number, and an existing state-token is replaced. The file is rewritten as one indented JSON object, so its key order and spacing may change. The new file replaces the old one in a single step and keeps the old file's permissions, so a failure leaves the old file or the new one and never half of each. The receipt is the same with the switch and without it.
What you see when something is wrong:

A preview creates nothing, and an external signer's registry does not exist until its bundle is submitted, so neither has a name to keep. With --preview, or with --wallet-address and --bundle, the switch is refused in one sentence, with exit status 2, before a wallet is opened or the chain is read.

A settings file that exists and cannot be written, or a missing one in a folder that cannot be written, is refused with exit status 2, naming the file and the cause, before a wallet is opened or the chain is read. Nothing is spent.
A create whose outcome is not success writes nothing: its receipt names whatever state there is.
If the write fails after the registry exists, one sentence on standard error says so, names the file and the cause, and says the state token is in the receipt. The exit status stays the create's own.
The switch has no variable and no key of the config file, because it is an action of one command and not a setting that stands. Every other command refuses it by name.

the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.text: The vault from the environment or the file.

As an operator who signs with a vault, you can name it once: SINGULAR_VAULT=alice.vault, or "vault": "alice.vault" in the config file, and open-datum insert --key alice --payload payload.json signs from it. The passphrase is not part of this: it stays on the terminal prompt, or on the descriptor --passphrase-fd names on the command, with a vault from either source just as with a typed one. A development network can also take it from the environment, as the next section says.

A write is signed by exactly one signer, so a vault you did not type on the command never joins another signer you did. If the line names the key file --wallet-skey, or an external signer with --wallet-address or --bundle, the command is refused in one sentence that names where the vault comes from and the flag on the line, before anything is read or sent:

For a vault from the file, the sentence names the key and the file (the "vault" key of singular.json) and says to remove the key. A preview signs nothing, so it takes no vault from the environment or the file, and --preview --wallet-address ADDR means the same with or without one. The wallet commands wallet create, wallet address and wallet sign take the vault from either source too: wallet create still refuses a path that is taken before it asks for a passphrase.

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: The passphrase from the environment on a development network.

As a reader of the tutorial on a private development network, I sign with a deliberately weak passphrase and do not want to type it at every command. I export it once, and every command that opens a vault reads it, with the other settings given as the sections above describe:

wallet create takes the variable for both of its asks, so a creation is not asked to confirm. A development network is any network that is not one of the three public ones the build names: mainnet (network magic 764824073), preprod (1) and preview (2). On those three, a command that would read the variable is refused in one sentence that names the variable and the network, before the vault is read. The sentence is the line a wallet command prints on standard error and the reason in the receipt of a write that was refused by the client:

The decision uses the network magic the command already receives. wallet sign is offline and takes no network magic, so it uses the network the bundle names, once it has read the bundle and before it reads the vault. A write is refused on mainnet before any passphrase is considered, so for a write the variable is refused on preprod and preview.

The variable is the whole of this: there is no config key for it and no flag, and a config file that names a passphrase is refused. The descriptor wins: with --passphrase-fd N on the command the variable is not read, on any network. With neither, the prompt is as before. A variable that is set but empty is refused, naming the variable, rather than taken as an empty passphrase.

The variable is for a passphrase that protects nothing. Every process you start inherits your environment, and a process of your account can read it, so a real vault keeps the prompt or the descriptor.

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: Keeping your signing key in an encrypted vault.

As Alice, I keep my payment signing key in one encrypted file instead of a plaintext key on disk. I run singular wallet create naming a new vault and a network, type a passphrase twice, and see my address on one line:

My key exists only inside that file: nothing else is written, no public part is kept beside it, and reading my address later means opening the vault — the same address prints, from the same passphrase:
A script supplies the passphrase on an inherited file descriptor, one line, and is never asked for a confirmation:

On a development network a script can set SINGULAR_PASSPHRASE instead, which a descriptor outranks; preprod and the other public networks refuse the variable (see the passphrase from the environment).

Creating over an existing path — a symbolic link included — is refused before a passphrase is asked for, with that path's bytes untouched; wallet address on a vault that is not there or cannot be read says so in one sentence naming the file, also before it asks for a passphrase; the vault file is made readable by its owner only, and a write that fails removes the file it made. A wrong passphrase, a corrupt file and a file that is not a vault all answer one refusal naming no secret, nothing prints on standard output, and the empty passphrase is refused at birth. Every creation draws a fresh key from the operating system's entropy: fresh entropy for every vault.

The vault is an ordinary age file, one passphrase recipient with scrypt work factor 18, holding the key's standard text envelope as its plaintext. Any age tool opens it with the passphrase and yields the envelope: age --decrypt alice.vault asks for the passphrase on the terminal and prints the plaintext, and the decrypted bytes are the cardano-cli key format itself, accepted wherever a signing-key file is read.

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: Signing a bundle of unsigned transactions offline.

As Bob, I receive a bundle of unsigned transactions from a writer — one JSON file — and I run singular wallet sign on an offline machine, naming my vault and the bundle. I type my passphrase once and get one witness file per transaction, with the paths on standard output and a short summary of what I signed on standard error:

The writer's side is a singular state create run, or an open-datum create, insert, update, terminate or fold run, that names --wallet-address and --bundle in place of the signing key: it builds its whole run as one bundle in build order, signs and sends nothing, states its own fields under expected in its receipt, and exits with status 19, waiting-for-signatures.

The bundle names the network it is built for, so no network setting is taken: every provider and registry option is refused by name, and the command opens no connection — it reads nothing but the bundle file, the vault file and the passphrase. A bundle is refused by name, and nothing is written, when a recorded identity is not the hash of its transaction's body, a recorded deadline is not the body's validity upper bound, an identity names two transactions, a key hash a body requires is covered by no signer address, or the vault's own address is not among the signers. A witness file that already exists is refused with its bytes untouched.

Each witness is the standard TxWitness ConwayEra text envelope of one verification-key witness — my public key and my signature over that transaction's own hash — so the submitting command (or any Cardano tool) can check and assemble them. The effects lines a bundle carries are the writer's claims: the summary shows them, and nothing trusts them. The registry a bundle names is the writer's statement too: the summary says so beside the name, and singular submit is where the bundle meets the chain. Whether the signers list is complete cannot be checked offline — inputs cannot be resolved — and expiry is not judged without a clock that knows the slot; both are the submitting command's judgement. No output, refusal or file names the passphrase or any key byte.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: As Bob, I hand back the witnesses for a bundle and run singular submit with the node settings and, when the bundle names a registry, the release that registry was created under. The transactions are sent in the bundle's order, and the receipt says what the chain shows. If the run is cut short, I run the same command again: it sends only the transactions the chain does not hold yet. If a body has expired, it says to rebuild the bundle and sends nothing. It needs no wallet key and keeps no state.

A bundle that names a registry is checked against it before anything else is read from the chain. The command resolves that registry with the release the bundle was created under, the blueprint I give, and compares its pinned policies exactly as every other command does: a registry whose pins differ is refused naming the field, the refusal is a client refusal with the cause registry-pin-mismatch and an empty list of submissions, and nothing is sent. The older bundles still submit, because the bundle format is unchanged and the release I give is the one the registry was created under. A bundle that names a registry and comes with no release is refused, cause release-not-given, before the chain is read. A bundle that names no registry is refused, cause bundle-names-no-registry, unless it is a create bundle: a create bundle names none because its registry does not exist until it is sent, and it needs no release. Without this refusal a writer could drop the name from a bundle to skip the comparison. The registry name in a bundle is its writer's statement, and wallet sign says so in its summary: submit checks the registry the bundle names, not that its transactions act on it. The receipt carries the standing of the application pin, applicationPin, once.

The witness files are the ones singular wallet sign writes; a directory stands for the .witness files it holds, and each witness is matched to a transaction by its signature, never by its file name. The command checks everything it can before it sends anything, in this order. Without touching the chain, it refuses a bundle the signing step would refuse, a bundle that names no registry and is not a create bundle, a bundle that names a registry when no release is given, a witness file it cannot read, and a witness whose signature verifies against no transaction of the bundle. Then it resolves the registry the bundle names and compares its pinned policies. Then it reads the chain once: where each transaction sits, the tip, and the inputs of each transaction not on chain yet — an input an earlier transaction of the bundle produces is taken from that transaction, every other from the chain. Witnesses are required for the transactions this run will send, and for those alone. It refuses a witness for a key none of them needs, a transaction left without a witness for a key it needs (its required signers and the payment keys of what it spends), an input found nowhere, and a transaction not on chain whose validity upper bound the tip has reached, with the word rebuild. A refusal exits as a client refusal, naming its cause, with an empty list of submissions.

A transaction the chain already holds, found by its identity, is skipped before those checks, and the witnesses supplied for it are ignored: the inputs it spent can no longer be read from the chain, and it is never sent again. A witness that cannot be read, or that verifies against no transaction of the bundle, is refused all the same, before the chain is read, even when every transaction is already on chain.

Each transaction the chain does not hold is sent in turn, carrying exactly its own witnesses, and confirmed before the next. An answer that may or may not mean the node took the transaction stops the run as partial, and nothing is sent again within the run; the next run finds what landed. Once every transaction is on chain, the receipt is read back from the chain: for each transaction, whether this run sent it or found it, its chain point, its confirmations, and each of its outputs — unspent with what it holds, or spent since — plus the bundle's hash.

The effect lines a bundle carries are its writer's claims: the receipt shows them under claims and never says they were confirmed. The completeness of the signatures is judged here, against the inputs the chain resolves, which the offline signing step cannot do. Expiry is judged against the tip read before the first send. A command that stops leaves nothing behind but its receipt, and it never resubmits on its own. A valid signature by an unneeded key over an already-landed body is not reported.

signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-v.text: Signing a write elsewhere, or from your vault.

As Bob, I keep my key away from the machine that talks to the node. I run a write of open datum naming my address and a new bundle file in place of the signing key. The command builds its whole run as one bundle of unsigned transactions, signs and sends nothing, and exits with status 19, waiting-for-signatures. I sign the bundle with singular wallet sign and send it with singular submit.

As Alice, I name my vault instead. I type my passphrase once, or hand it over through a descriptor in a script. The command builds the same bundle, signs every transaction from the vault, and sends them in order as singular submit does. Its receipt reads what the chain shows.
A write takes exactly one signer:
Alice starts open-datum fold naming her vault. Before any other read, the command opens it once and receives the signing key in memory only.

The command reads the registry and builds the whole run as one bundle, saves it and journals one waiting line per transaction, then signs every transaction from the vault. It sends them in order as singular submit does. Each member found on chain is journalled landed, and Alice receives the receipt read from the chain.

The address must pay a key: a script address is refused, naming it. A vault, an address and a key file are three signers, and naming two of them is refused. A passphrase descriptor without a vault is refused too. A wrong passphrase or an unreadable vault is refused, naming the vault, before anything else is read or written. No receipt, journal line, trace or error carries the passphrase or a key byte.

what-each-receipt-says.text: Your vault: the outcome of the submission, the bundle, and per transaction the submit core's chain facts under submissions. When every transaction has landed, the command's fields are stated as fact. Otherwise they stay under expected. When the node refuses a transaction, the run ends as a ledger refusal, and wentThrough names the transactions that landed before it.

Signing elsewhere: the outcome waiting-for-signatures and the bundle. That is its hash, the written and the saved path, the signer, and per transaction its step, identity, deadline and effect lines. The command's own fields sit under expected, because nothing has landed yet.
A key file (being retired): the receipt it has always printed.

Status 19 also ends any write that a pending bundle stops before it builds anything. Its receipt names that bundle under pendingBundle: its hash, its saved path, and the transactions still awaited with their deadlines. Recovering a registry command follows a bundle from there.

A pending bundle stops the next write of the same registry by the same wallet only. A write in another registry, a create of a new registry included, is not stopped, and it may spend a wallet output that the pending bundle needs.

A bundle whose transactions carry a deadline then dies by expiry, and running the command again rebuilds it. A bundle signed elsewhere whose transactions carry none, an open-datum insert, update or terminate without --fold and a create, never expires: if it can never land, it keeps stopping the next write of that registry by that wallet at status 19. The way out today is, for a create, a create that names another output with --seed, as When a bundle waits for signatures says; for the others, --state-dir naming another state directory, which starts a fresh journal for that registry and wallet.

how-long-a-bundle-can-wait.text: How long a bundle can wait.
A bundle can be sent until the first deadline of its transactions. The builders' validity bounds are unchanged by signing elsewhere. Each command's builder may choose at most this deadline:

A builder can choose an earlier bound. It takes a near one when the end of a window cannot be translated to a slot yet, and it never goes past the ledger's horizon. So the deadline a transaction actually carries is the one the receipt prints for it, deadline per transaction, and it can be only seconds or minutes after the build: sign and send before that printed deadline.

A pending create bundle blocks its own state directory only, which is keyed by the network, the token it will mint and the wallet. A second create from the same wallet and seed waits for it. So does one without --seed while the same output is unspent, because it picks that output again. A create naming another output with --seed makes a different registry, which nothing blocks, and the pending create's journal stays as a record.

naming-the-registry.text: As an application operator, use the state token and registry address returned by the creation command. The commands on the proved design are documented in creating a registry and registering keys. The former singular registry routes have been retired. Reading the new line is tracked separately in issue 744.

choosing-a-registrys-windows.text: As a registry creator, you choose the processing and retract windows when you run open-datum create, through --process-time MS and --retract-time MS. Each must be a positive integer number of milliseconds; any other value is refused before the command builds or signs anything. When omitted, they are 600 000 and 300 000 milliseconds: ten minutes to fold a booked request, then five minutes for its owner to reclaim it.

Both windows are written into the state datum and fixed for the life of the registry. A later command cannot change them. The successful create receipt and inspect report processTime and retractTime read from that datum; booking deadlines follow the registry's actual windows, including those of a registry created before these defaults changed. The defaults give public network reads and folds more time; development-network CI explicitly creates its throwaway registries with shorter windows.

booking-and-folding.text: An insert or a terminate books a request and stops. The request waits at the registry; the command's receipt names it, the booking's transaction, and the fold deadline — the request's submission time plus the registry's processing time — as a POSIX time, and as a slot when pinned time converts it. Nothing is folded, and the registry's root, its mirror and its saved state do not move.

Before anything is signed, insert, update and terminate check the key's current entry: a booking the entry rules out is refused with the key and a named reason. An insert of a key that is already registered, or already retired, is refused; an update or a terminate of a key that is not registered, or already retired, is refused. The refusal is labelled client policy in the receipt, and it runs the same way in planning, in preview and live. The fold still validates every booking it folds, so a booking made through the permissive builders can still reach the chain's own refusal at the fold.

open-datum fold folds pending requests. It is an ordinary command: it signs and funds with the wallet it is given, journals its own transactions, and may be run by any wallet, not only the one that booked. An insertion's request carries the envelope its fold delivers, so the folder reads it from the pending request on the chain; nothing the booking wrote to its own state directory is needed.

The requester books with its wallet. The folder reads that pending request, then builds, signs and funds the fold with the folder's wallet; the saved registry journal, mirror and state follow the observed fold:

As Carol, I fold with whatever wallet I have. fold, reject and reclaim fund and collateralise from an ada-only output of my wallet that carries no reference script. When my wallet holds none it can use — every output I may spend carries tokens, or is too small — the command first spends one transaction of its own to prepare a funding output: ada only, made as the transaction's first output, with everything else the spent outputs held returned to me in a remainder, tokens included, and no reference script ever spent. An output that publishes a script is never spent, so it never funds a preparation: a wallet holding only such outputs has nothing to spend and is refused for that. The preparation is journalled under the command's name like any other transaction, and the receipt names it; a wallet that already holds a usable output gets no preparation at all. insert, terminate and update of the open-datum application do the same from the same wallet: their --preview shows the preparation (its transaction, the lovelace of its funding output and its fee) or says that none is needed, and submits and journals nothing, and their receipt carries a preparation entry only when one was made. When my wallet cannot pay for both the preparation and the command, the command refuses before signing anything, naming what is needed and what I hold, and submits nothing. The allowance --max-outlay is judged against the command and the fee of the preparation before anything is signed, and once more after the preparation is confirmed, on the command rebuilt from a fresh read of the wallet: when that outlay passes the allowance, the preparation stands confirmed, the command is not signed, and the refusal says so. Naming an output with --fund-input is final: it is used as it is when it suits, and refused with today's text when it does not.

open-datum fold judges each pending request on its own — against the registry's live state, the host clock and the application's rules — and settles every request that passes, up to the capacity bound, in ledger input order, at most one per key. Two users who book at the same moment are settled by one fold. The receipt's capacity field states the bound, 9, with its provenance: an estimate, not a measurement, of how many requests fit in a fold. A request past the bound is named capacity and is for the next fold. A fold is never refused because several requests are pending. The fold folds insertActive and updateTerminal; any other edge is refused edge-inadmissible in the model's words.

Every request the fold leaves out is named in the receipt with its reason and where the reason comes from. Nine reasons are the model's own refusal words, reported verbatim; five are the processor's own selection policy, which the model has no counterpart for. The table lists all fourteen names by source.

A request refused in the model's words failed the model's own check — its edge, its window, its approval, or its leaf against the live state — and stays refused while the state still rules it out. The window check asks the model's admission at the probe bound the folder would build under, the clock plus the thirty seconds a fold needs to be included: a bound past the request's deadline is refused not-phase1, and a bound equal to the deadline admits, as the chain admits it. A request left out by selection policy failed the processor's own rule: it does not decode as a request; its carried datum does not read, or, for a termination under the neutral value, the value carries no holding rules and the detail names the application's own executable; an earlier included request already names its key; or the fold is at its capacity bound. A request named capacity is for the next fold. A request refused not-phase1 stays pending. The former generic retraction and rejection commands have been retired.

The receipt no longer carries the single-request fields it once printed at the top level: request, key, edge, liveOutput, envelope, released and deposit, and the datum hash and datum bytes of a datum delivery, are gone. Each fact about a settled request is read from its entry in settled: its request, key, edge, owner, settlement and deadline, where the settlement carries the live output and the envelope, or the datum hash and bytes, or the released output and the deposit. What stays at the top level are the facts of the transaction: the folder, the fold transaction, the root, the fold deadline, the validity bound slot, the post-build verdict, the host clock and the time remaining, then the three lists. settled names each settled request in ledger order; excluded names each left-out request with its request, reason, source and detail, in ledger order; capacity states the bound with its provenance. The example shows the lists with two pending requests of which one is left out: the first settles, the second is named with its reason and source, and the capacity states the bound of 9 with its provenance.

--request R is an expectation: the command is refused unless R is among the settled requests. The refusal names why R is not settled: R's own reason and source when R is pending but left out, or that R is not pending — folded, retracted or never booked. With pending requests but nothing settleable, the command is refused nothing-to-fold, naming every exclusion with its reason and source. With nothing pending it says so: nothing is pending and there is no request to fold. Past its window means past the processing deadline as the probe bound reads it: the bound the folder would build under, the clock plus the thirty seconds a fold needs to be included, past the request's deadline.

insert --fold and terminate --fold, which run through the open-datum executable since the command-line split, take the same selection and print the same lists as open-datum fold. The fold-derived facts are no longer printed beside them: the live output, the envelope, the released output and the deposit are read from the entry for the request they just booked in settled. What the combined forms keep of their own is the booking's key fields, the booking transaction, the fold transaction and the root. If the request the command just booked is left out, the command stops partial: the booking is confirmed and its request stays pending, named with the reason.

Before anything is signed the command still refuses the outlay past --max-outlay and a funding output that is not the wallet's. When a preparation is needed, the outlay counts its fee; once the preparation is confirmed the outlay of the command, rebuilt from a fresh read of the wallet, is judged again, and a command past the allowance is not signed: the refusal says that the preparation stands confirmed.

A booking wallet is judged on what the booking costs. Opening a write session applies no wallet threshold. Before anything is built, a wallet holding less than the fold reserve (from the network parameters and the reference scripts the fold reads) is refused, and a wallet that holds nothing it may spend at all, or whose --fund-input is not among its ada-only outputs, is refused. A wallet whose spendable outputs all carry tokens is not refused for that: the command prepares the funding output it needs, as above. Outputs that publish a script are never spent, so a wallet holding only those holds nothing it may spend and is refused as such. After the booking is built and before it is signed, a wallet holding less than the measured outlay (its fee, the bond its request locks, the bound on the fold that follows and, when a preparation was needed, the fee of the preparation) is refused. The shortfall refusal is client-refusal and carries the wallet address, what it holds, what is required, the shortfall, the UTxO count and that the policy is the client's; requiredIs says what is required: the fold reserve, the measured outlay, or the preparation. For the fold reserve and the measured outlay the reason ends (client policy). For the preparation, reached when the wallet cannot pay for the command and the preparation it needs, the reason begins preparation-unfunded, names what the command needs, the fee of the preparation and its remainder floor, and ends (client policy); nothing was submitted; that refusal also carries the fee, the remainder floor and the largest output the wallet may spend. An empty wallet or a foreign funding output is refused as client-refusal with (client policy), carrying the wallet address, the UTxO count, what it holds and the client policy, and no required or shortfall. The empty-wallet refusal ends with the faucet step — Fund this address, then rerun. On preprod the faucet is https://docs.cardano.org/cardano-testnets/tools/faucet. One funded output is enough: nothing is split by hand, and every write spends the wallet's largest ada-only output and returns its change, or first prepares one from what the wallet holds. The foreign funding choice does not end with the faucet step. Preview and write judge the same wallet at the same points in the same order. update is judged the same way with its own fee as the outlay: it has no fold to pay for, so no fold reserve is asked of it, and a wallet that cannot pay for the update and its preparation is refused before anything is signed, naming what is needed and what the wallet holds; --max-outlay below the update's outlay plus the preparation's fee is refused before anything is signed, naming both amounts and ending (client policy); nothing was submitted; the same allowance is judged again once the preparation is confirmed, and a command past it is not signed, the reason then ending (client policy); the preparation, the output it made, stands confirmed and the command was not signed. fold and create get no further measured judgement: a build that succeeds proves the wallet pays the fee, and a wallet that needs a preparation it cannot pay for is refused with the same shortfall.

That check is the fast refusal, not the proof. After the fold is built and before it is signed, its validity upper bound is judged again from the built body and the host clock: the bound must be at or before the slot of the deadline when pinned time converts it, or, when it does not, must begin at or before the deadline time; a bound pinned time cannot convert, or a clock that has meanwhile come within the margin, is refused unsigned, with the bound, the clock and the deadline in the receipt.
The deadline the fold is judged against is the earliest among the settled requests, each as its booking's receipt states. A fold refused for it submitted nothing, and pending requests stay pending.

What this page still does not claim, stated plainly: the capacity of 9 is an estimate, not measured on a real network, and this page claims no preprod number; measuring it belongs to #530. Recovery of a fold of several requests is proved by unit-level checks, and the interruption of such a fold on a development network is not executed yet. One fold's batch is compared by the state, mint and payments it reaches, never by a model transaction it does not build; folding requests together is not shown equal to folding them apart, and two orders are not shown to give equal roots. For a batch with two different defects the model names the edge set, then the window, then the law, while the chain checks each request's window beside its law, so the first reason can differ and no live row compares such a batch. A retraction still carries its own submission time until its admission moves onto the request's.

what-a-write-records.text: As a registry operator, you can identify the session and raw facts used for a prepared transaction, and distinguish them from its submission and later confirmation. Shared HTTP sessions are Unbound: several reads in one session may observe different chain states. Every supplied fact is explicitly Unverified with NoVerifierConfigured; no witness verifies it.

A prepared receipt carries the actual acquisition identity, fact/verdict extent and raw-source records. Its chain-point field is empty for an Unbound session. An inspect or confirmation tip is a separate observation, not proof that the prepared reads belonged to that block. A provider's facts also cannot override the ledger's refusal of a transaction.

Confirmation waits for the exact transaction output, rather than a status flag alone. With an upper validity bound, its provider deadline is the POSIX start of that slot plus 120 seconds; with no upper bound, it is now plus 300 seconds. The CLI's --confirm-timeout also bounds its wait. The latest observed block can establish expiry. An unresolved submission remains journalled and is not sent again by recovery.

choosing-a-usable-validity-interval.text: As a caller building under load, you want a usable interval before construction starts. The builder selects bounds only when at least ten seconds of usable slots remain at its observed tip. Build duration and later provider observations can consume that interval; this selection does not guarantee ledger acceptance. Floor, ceiling and slot-start conversions use the pinned genesis/history, with only the final era's end opened. A time before genesis refuses TimeBeforeHistory; a fresh protocol major that differs from the pin refuses EraBeyondPinned before construction.

The moving ledger horizon is the first epoch boundary at or after the observed tip plus the authenticated consensus buffer. The selected upper is the smaller of the registry's original upper and the horizon minus one. The usable lower is the larger of the actual finite lower and tip plus one; an omitted body lower stays omitted.

An empty interval refuses WindowPastLedgerHorizon. A nonempty registry-limited interval shorter than ten seconds refuses WindowTooShort without waiting. If the horizon alone shortens an otherwise longer window, the builder waits once for a later horizon before constructing the body. The wait is bounded by ten seconds of slots and 20 seconds of wall time; a stalled horizon refuses HorizonWaitTimedOut with the last observed tip and horizon. The wait is logged and neither signs nor submits anything. These observations remain Unbound.

following-what-a-command-does.text: As a registry operator, you can watch a command take its protocol steps while it runs, and keep the same account as data. Every command narrates one stream of events: at --trace what, the registry it attached, each key and request it read, the edge action it takes on them and its result; at --trace how, also the mechanics under each step, each with its time. Standard output still carries the receipt alone, so a script reading the receipt is unaffected by any narration.
On a terminal a command narrates what to standard error unless told otherwise. A fold, narrated at how:

Each line is indented by where it happened: the registry, then the key or request, then the edge action, with each mechanic under the action it belongs to. Identifiers are shortened in text; amounts are in tADA. A failure says where it happened, and the four places are distinct: refused by the client before anything was submitted, refused by local script evaluation before anything was submitted, rejected by the ledger, or refused by the provider, so that no ledger judged the transaction.

With --trace-format json, or a file:PATH sink, each event is one JSON object on its own line, written as it happens: its level (what or how), its scope (the registry, key, request, edge action and transaction it happened in, outermost first) and its event with that event's fields, in full. The last line of every stream is command-ended, naming the command, the outcome class of its receipt and its elapsed time. Keys are written in base16, and no event carries a signing key or the text of a failure: a failure names only its type.

A sink that cannot be written, a closed standard error or a full disk loses that sink's narration and nothing else: the other sinks, the receipt, the journal and the exit status are as they would be with no narration at all.

when-the-provider-cannot-be-used.text: When the provider cannot be used.

reading-through-an-index.text: The former --backend node / --backend indexer comparison is retired. Ordinary commands use the Koios path only. They do not create an in-memory chain index or accept an ordinary node socket: the production node read adapter and the in-memory indexer are removed with the provider migration, and no registry command names a node backend. Private generated nodes and independent LSQ probes remain test harness components behind the private facade; none of them ships with the terminal.

An index must not fabricate transaction history for genesis-only allocations. The retained private genesis-only control uses genuine initial ledger outputs and refuses coverage-incomplete, naming their output references, with exit 12 and no registry write. Funding those allocations through a real transaction creates full-block history that the accepting control can read. This is a private source control, not a promise that every remote service detects all missing history. Missing or inconsistent registry reconstruction remains a refusal and must not become an empty registry.

public-environment-configuration.text: As an operator, I can supply each setting of the section above as a variable, for example SINGULAR_STATE_TOKEN when I omit --state-token; an explicit command-line value takes precedence, and the config file comes after the variable. The token names the registry, and never selects a provider. SINGULAR_CONFIG names the config file. SINGULAR_LOG=PATH appends phase events to a file alongside the narration sinks selected by --trace, --trace-to and --trace-format. It does not replace those sinks or change their command-line precedence. An empty phase-log path disables that sink.

harness-appendix-test-hooks.text: Released singular and open-datum binaries carry no fault-injection or hidden trie-diagnostic hooks.
